docupedia_results.full_body:
EPC-VN's automation and AI tools are written in Python. Unless compiled and finalized, most tools are constantly under active development and will be provided as python scripts. In order to run these scripts, ensure a functional environment has been setup on your computer.

Table of contents

1. Installation

Press the Windows key on the keyboard.

Search for IT Workplace Toolkit.

Click to open IT Workplace Toolkit.

Go to the Add/Remove Software section on the IT Service Portal.

Tick to install the latest version of Anaconda Python.

Tick to install Microsoft Visual Studio Code with Proxy Configuration (PX).

Both requested software are free of charge.

Write your Reason for Request.

Click Request.

Wait up to 2 days to receive an email approving your request.

At least 20 minutes after receiving the email, click Check Now in the IT Workplace Toolkit to fetch the latest software updates.

Go to Software Center to begin installing Anaconda Python and VSCode.

When the installation has finished, restart your computer.

2. Running a Python Script

Press the Windows key on the keyboard.

Search for Anaconda Navigator (Anaconda3).

Click to open Anaconda Navigator (Anaconda3). It will take some time to open.

Launch VS Code from within Anaconda Navigator.

Opening VS Code outside of Anaconda Navigator will not work.

To install libraries and modules, open a terminal in VS Code (Ctrl+`).

Using a terminal outside of VS Code will not work.

Use pip commands.

Open the folder containing the Python script in VS Code (Ctrl+K Ctrl+O).

Edit the script if needed.

Run the script without debugging (Ctrl+F5 or click the triangle button at the top right.

Alternatively, debug the script (F5).

3. Troubleshooting

For assistance or troubleshooting, contact Nguyen Van Khanh (PS/EPC1-VN) or Ton That Khac Trinh (PS/EPC1-VN).

docupedia_results.full_body:
This guide will walk you through the process of setting up a robust and isolated development environment using Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2), Visual Studio Code, and Dev Containers. You'll learn how to install WSL2, clone a repository, deploy a Dev Container, manage dependencies, and build your project, all within a consistent and reproducible environment.

Table of Contents

Prerequisites

Before you begin, ensure you have the following:

  • Windows 10 Version 2004 or higher (Build 19041 or higher), or Windows 11.
  • Administrator privileges on your Windows machine (for WSL2 installation).
  • An access token for the following servers:
    • artifactory.boschdevcloud.com
    • artifactory-02.boschdevcloud.com
    • rb-artifactory.bosch.com
    • github.boschdevcloud.com
    • sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com
    • sourcecode01.de.bosch.com (tbd)

Step-by-Step Guide

Follow these steps carefully to set up your development environment.

Step 1: Install and Configure WSL2

For this step you need to install a Bosch internal WSL Linux distribution.

Enable WSL and Virtual Machine Platform

Open PowerShell or Command Prompt as Administrator and run the following commands:

PowerShell
dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux /all
dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:VirtualMachinePlatform /all

Restart your computer after running these commands to apply the changes.

Install Linux Distribution

  • After restarting, open the WSL linux distribution folder:

\\bosch.com\dfsrb\DfsDE\DIV\XC\Engineering\x_domain\linux\WSL

  • Select the latest stable release folder and copy it to your desktop:

  • Open the downloaded folder and run _Installer_.exe as administrator:

  • The installer will open the following window, just click on Next:

 

  • Accept the compliance agreement, overwrite the current WSL settings (Recommended) and click on Setup WSL

  • The installation script will rise the following question, just type A + ENTER to bypass all warnings:

  • Wait a few minutes for the installation. At the end you will get the following message:

  • The installation created a link in your desktop, so just open it:

  • A shell window to your WSL instance will be open, wait a few seconds and hit ENTER until you have internet+docker: ok:

  • A second window with the WSL PX Monitor will also be opened. Do not close that window, just minimize it:

  • Open your home folder by using the Windows File Explorer \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu-22.04\home\<user>:

  • Open the .bashrc file with a text editor and add the following content at the end of the file:
.bashrc file
## DOUBLE CHECK THAT THESE EXPORTS ARE REQUIRED. IF LEFT LIKE THIS THEY CAUSE ISSUES ##
export ARTIFACTORY_BCN_TOKEN=<your-artifactory-bcn-token from rb-artifactory.bosch.com>
export ARTIFACTORY_BDC_TOKEN=<your-artifactory-bdc-token from artifactory.boschdevcloud.com>
export ARTIFACTORY02_BDC_TOKEN=<your-artifactory-bdc02-token from artifactory-02.boschdevcloud.com>
export GH_TOKEN=<your-github-token from github.boschdevcloud.com>
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ##
	
export CONTAINER_UID=$(id -u) && export CONTAINER_GID=$(id -g) && export CONTAINER_USER=$(whoami)
	
alias sde='.devcontainer/initialize-command.sh && docker compose build --pull dev-env && docker compose run --rm dev-env ".devcontainer/post-start-command.sh && \$0"'
alias docker-compose='docker compose'

You have to include here the tokens from the Prerequisites.

  • In the same folder, create a file called .netrc, open it with a text editor, copy the following content and save it in Unix format:
.netrc file
machine artifactory.boschdevcloud.com
	login <user>
	password <your-token from artifactory.boschdevcloud.com>
 
machine artifactory-02.boschdevcloud.com
	login <user>@bosch.com
	password <your-token from artifactory-02.boschdevcloud.com>
 
machine rb-artifactory.bosch.com
	login <user>
	password <your-token from rb-artifactory.bosch.com>

machine github.boschdevcloud.com
	login <user>
	password <your-token from github.boschdevcloud.com>

machine sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com
	login <user>
	password <your-token from sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com>

You have to include here the tokens from the Prerequisites. Notice the artifactory-02.boschdevcloud.com is the only server that requires a username with the format <user>@bosch.com.

  • Now reboot your wsl instance by sending the exit command. It will close the WSL shell and the WSL PX Monitor windows. To ensure the WSL instance is completelly off, open a PowerShell window and send the wsl --shutdown command:

Step 2: Clone the STIL project repositories and deploy the dev container.

  • Open your Development WSL2 Linux Distribution:

  • You need to install some dependencies, so run the following commands:
WSL
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git-lfs jq python-is-python3 -y
  • Create a folder called "repos" in your home:
WSL
mkdir ~/repos
  • Now clone your projects, for STIL project you have the following clone commands, just clone the repositories you really need to save space in your storage drive:
WSL
git clone --recursive -b develop https://sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com/scm/ra6_stil/stilcore.git ~/repos/stilcore
git clone --recursive -b develop https://sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com/scm/ra6_stil/tsw_rid15.git ~/repos/tsw_rid15
git clone --recursive -b develop https://sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com/scm/ra6_stil/tsw_rid30.git ~/repos/tsw_rid30
git clone --recursive -b develop https://sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com/scm/ra6_stil/tsw_rid40.git ~/repos/tsw_rid40
git clone --recursive -b develop https://sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com/scm/ra6_stil/tsw_rid70.git ~/repos/tsw_rid70
git clone --recursive -b develop https://sourcecode06.dev.bosch.com/scm/ra6_stil/tsw_rid71.git ~/repos/tsw_rid71

Let's use the tsw_rid15 repository as example for the next steps. You should change the folder name in the commands if applies.

  • Wait until the clone is complete and then move to the tsw_rid15 folder and run the sde command:

WSL
cd ~/repos/tsw_rid15
sde

The sde command (defined in the .bashr file), will pull the docker image from the server (>10GB) and build the container, so it's expected to take several minutes when you run it for the first time, just be patient until it finishes.

if you experience network instabilities (EOF error) just stop the wsl-network service and try the sde command again.

sudo systemctl stop wsl-network.service


If you get a git-related error during the sde command, such as fatal: Remote branch 'X.Y.Z?' not found in upstream origin, it is likely caused by incorrect line endings in the conanconf_version.txt file.

This can be fixed by converting the file to Unix-style line endings. Run the following command from your repository root:

dos2unix conanconf_version.txt

If you get the following permission error:

You need to manually enter in the container and set the permissions, then you can run the sde command again:

docker compose run --rm dev-env /bin/bash
sudo chown -R $USER:$USER ~/.conan2
exit



Step 3: Open the repository in the dev container and build.

Dev Containers allow you to define a fully reproducible development environment in code, ensuring everyone on your team has the same tools, dependencies, and settings.

Understanding Dev Containers

A Dev Container is a Docker container configured with specific tools, runtimes, and dependencies required for your project. This configuration is defined in a .devcontainer folder at the root of your repository, typically containing a devcontainer.json file and a Dockerfile.

Open the Repository with VS Code

  • If you skipped the Step3, then you need to open VS Code in your windows PC and then connect to WSL:

  • Install the Dev Containers extension if not installed:

  • Type CTRL+SHIFT+P , then Open Folder in Container and select your project folder:

Visual Studio Code will install the required extensions automatically, so this procedure takes some time when you do it for the first time, just be patient until it finishes.

First Time Setup

Remote conan packages

  • Type CTRL+SHIFT+P , then Run Task, Conan Install and select the proper conan profile.

For this example:

    • Gen6: AWR2E44 Build R5F
    • Gen7: SX601 Build M7

You should get the following output:

in case you get this output, then you need to local install the ECUif package:


Package ECUif (Optional)

This step is only required if the ECUif is not configured as remote conan package in the STIL Routine.

  • Open a terminal window in VSCode and clone the ECUif package:
git clone -b develop --recurse-submodules https://github.boschdevcloud.com/RA6/prj.ecu_if_sw.git ~/mnt/ws/tools/prj.ecu_if_sw
  • Open the ConanCommitIdEcuIfSwGenX.txt files in order to get the commit Ids for Gen6 and Gen7:

For this example:

    • Gen6 commit id: 28050bfe
    • Gen7 commit id: 383dcca4
  • Check the name of the conan profile for Gen6 and Gen7:

For this example:

    • Gen6 conan profile: tools/conan/profiles/STIL_awr2e44
    • Gen7 conan profile: tools/conan/profiles/STIL_sx601

If your ConanCommitIdEcuIfSwGenX.txt file contains a conan package version (i.e. 25.0.0) and not a commit ID, then the ECUif is already configured as a remote conan package in the STIL Routine.

Replace the commit ids and the conan profile files in the following commands according to the routine you are installing.

  • Enter in the package and create local branches for Gen6 and Gen7 with the respective commit id:
cd ~/mnt/ws/tools/prj.ecu_if_sw
git branch gen6 "28050bfe"
git branch gen7 "383dcca4"
  • Switch to Gen6 branch and install the conan package associated to the Gen6 profile:
git switch --recurse-submodules gen6
conan editable add . --name=rb_ecu_if_sw --version=28050bfe --user=ra --channel=stil_local
conan install . -o variant=r5f_awr2e44_b2_pf -pr=../conan/profiles/STIL_awr2e44 --build=missing --no-remote
conan build . -o variant=r5f_awr2e44_b2_pf -pr=../conan/profiles/STIL_awr2e44
  • Back to the routine project and install the conan package associated to the Gen6 profile:
cd ~/mnt/ws
conan install . -pr=tools/conan/profiles/STIL_awr2e44 --build=missing --no-remote
  • Move to the ECUif package again and switch to Gen7 branch, then install the conan package associated to the Gen7 profile:
git switch --recurse-submodules gen7
conan editable add . --name=rb_ecu_if_sw --version=383dcca4 --user=ra --channel=stil_local
conan install . -o variant=sx601_b_single_core -pr=../conan/profiles/STIL_sx601 --build=missing --no-remote
conan build . -o variant=sx601_b_single_core -pr=../conan/profiles/STIL_sx601
  • Back again to the main project and install the conan package associated to the Gen7 profile:
cd ~/mnt/ws
conan install . -pr=tools/conan/profiles/STIL_sx601 --build=missing --no-remote

Switch between Gen6 and Gen7 projects

Configure local ECUif package for Gen6 and Gen7

This step is only required if the ECUif is not configured as remote conan package in the STIL Routine.

You must to do this steps for the first time and when switching between Gen6 and Gen7.

Gen6

cd ~/mnt/ws/tools/prj.ecu_if_sw
git switch --recurse-submodules gen6
conan build . -o variant=r5f_awr2e44_b2_pf -pr=../conan/profiles/STIL_awr2e44

Gen7

cd ~/mnt/ws/tools/prj.ecu_if_sw
git switch --recurse-submodules gen7
conan build . -o variant=sx601_b_single_core -pr=../conan/profiles/STIL_sx601

Notice you can skip the conan build command since the package is already built for Gen6 or Gen7 in a previous step, nevertheless is highly recommended to build every time you switch between Gen6 and Gen7, just to ensure it was built with the correct branch.

Execute the Build Command

  • Now you are able to build the routine, so type CTRL+SHIFT+P , then CMake: Clean Rebuild and select the proper preset.
    • Gen6: cnf_STIL_awr2e44_arm
    • Gen7: cnf_STIL_sx601_arm

You should get the following output:

You can check the output files:

Step 5: Congratulations! Your Development Environment is Ready

You've reached the end of this guide! At this point, you have a robust and isolated development environment set up with WSL2 and Dev Containers. You've learned how to:

  • Install and configure WSL2.
  • Clone a repository directly into your Linux environment.
  • Integrate Visual Studio Code with your Linux subsystem.
  • Install your project's dependencies.
  • Open your project in a Dev Container, ensuring a reproducible environment.
  • Build your project, verifying that everything works as expected.

This approach not only enhances the performance of your development tools on Windows but also standardizes your environment, facilitating team collaboration and ensuring that "it works on my machine" is a thing of the past.

Troubleshooting and Best Practices

if you experience network instabilities (EOF error) just stop the wsl-network service and try the sde command again.

sudo systemctl stop wsl-network.service

Copilot issues within WSL

  • If copilot works in host VSCode but does not load within WSL, try removing the proxy argument in VSCode settings:

  1. Open preferences menu
  2. Click on Settings
  3. Search for "proxy"
  4. Delete any preconfigured proxy setting

docupedia_results.full_body:
When running Azure or AWS services, or anything that requires making requests outside the Bosch network, we face problems with the corporate proxy.

The preferred solution is to install PX by BD via the IT Service Portal. The proxy runs in the background and handles authentication with the Bosch corporate proxy automatically.

Step-by-step guide

1. Method 1 - via IT Service Portal (most recommended)

    $b64 = [Convert]::ToBase64String($_.RawData, 'InsertLineBreaks')

StatusDescription : OK

4.1. ❌ Error: WinError 10061 — Connection refused

The proxy port 3128 is not available or is being used by another process. Check for conflicts:

netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING | findstr 3128

Get-Process -Id <PID> | Select-Object Id, ProcessName, Path

If a process other than px.exe is occupying port 3128, stop it:

Stop-Process -Id <PID> -Force

Then restart PX.

4.2. ❌ Environment variables not taking effect

If you set the variables but they are not being picked up, verify the current session has them:

echo $env:HTTP_PROXY

echo $env:HTTPS_PROXY


Both should return http://127.0.0.1:3128. If not, re-run the SetEnvironmentVariable commands and restart your terminal.

4.3. ❌ Error: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED on az login / Python requests

python -c "import requests,os; print(requests.get('https://management.azure.com/tenants?api-version=2020-01-01', verify=os.environ['REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE']).status_code)"

If login succeeds but "Retrieving tenants and subscriptions" fails, your bundle is missing a CA for that host — use the full bosch-full-ca.pem from 2.3, which covers all Bosch issuing CAs.

Send: python --version

Step 3 — Install Required Libraries

pip install pyserialpip install pyinstaller

pip install pillow

 
3. Communication Setup


The TOE 8951 uses SCPI-like commands via serial communication.

Key commands:

SYST:REM              → Enable remote control mode

VOLT <value>       → Set output voltage
CURR <value>      → Set current limit

OUTP ON              → Enable output
OUTP OFF             → Disable output

MEAS:VOLT?         → Read actual output voltage
MEAS:CURR?        → Read actual output current

*RST                      → Reset instrument to default state

PowerSupply_TOE_8951.py

import serial
import time
import tkinter as tk
import serial.tools.list_ports
from tkinter import messagebox
from PIL import Image, ImageTk



MAX_VOLTAGE = 60      # Adjust
MAX_CURRENT = 10      # Adjust

BAUD = 9600
PORT = "COM3"
ser = None

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# AUTO DETECT COM PORT
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
#def detect_port():
#    ports = list(serial.tools.list_ports.comports())
#    for p in ports:
#        return p.device
#    return None

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def connect():
    global ser

    try:
        ser = serial.Serial(PORT, BAUD, timeout=1)
        time.sleep(0.5)
        ser.write(b'SYST:REM ')
        status_label.config(text=f"Connected: {PORT}")
    except Exception as e:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", f"Connection failed: {e}")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# SEND COMMAND
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def send(cmd):
    if ser is None:
        messagebox.showerror("Error", "Not connected")
        return
    ser.write((cmd + " ").encode())

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# OUTPUT CONTROL
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def on():
    send("OUTP ON")
    led_canvas.itemconfig(led, fill="green")

def off():
    send("OUTP OFF")
    led_canvas.itemconfig(led, fill="red")

def reset():
    send("*RST")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# SET VOLTAGE AND CURRENT
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def set_values():
    try:
        voltage = float(voltage_entry.get())
        current = float(current_entry.get())

        if voltage < 0 or voltage > MAX_VOLTAGE:
            messagebox.showwarning("Voltage Error", f"Voltage must be between 0 and {MAX_VOLTAGE} V")
            return

        if current < 0 or current > MAX_CURRENT:
            messagebox.showwarning("Current Error", f"Current must be between 0 and {MAX_CURRENT} A")
            return

        send(f"VOLT {voltage}")
        send(f"CURR {current}")

        messagebox.showinfo("Success", "Voltage and Current Set Successfully")

    except ValueError:
        messagebox.showwarning("Input Error", "Please enter valid numeric values")


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# PRESETS
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

    voltage_entry.delete(0, tk.END)
    voltage_entry.insert(0, "5")
    current_entry.delete(0, tk.END)
    current_entry.insert(0, "1")

def preset_12v():
    voltage_entry.delete(0, tk.END)
    voltage_entry.insert(0, "12")
    current_entry.delete(0, tk.END)
    current_entry.insert(0, "2")

def preset_24v():
    voltage_entry.delete(0, tk.END)
    voltage_entry.insert(0, "24")
    current_entry.delete(0, tk.END)
    current_entry.insert(0, "3")

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# REAL-TIME MEASUREMENT
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def read_measurements():
    if ser:
        try:
            ser.write(b"MEAS:VOLT? ")
            voltage = ser.readline().decode().strip()

            ser.write(b"MEAS:CURR? ")
            current = ser.readline().decode().strip()

            meas_voltage_label.config(text=f"{voltage} V")
            meas_current_label.config(text=f"{current} A")
        except:
            pass
    root.after(1000, read_measurements)

root.geometry("700x260")

canvas.pack(fill="both", expand=True)

meas_voltage_label = tk.Label(root, text="0 V", font=("Arial", 14), bg="white")
meas_voltage_label.place(x=590, y=55)

docupedia_results.full_body:
Welcome to the official user guide for Skills in Ask Bosch Powered by Gemini Enterprise. This guide is designed to help business users, prompt engineers to understand, build, and deploy modular assistant capabilities across Bosch.

1. Overview: What are Skills?

In Gemini Enterprise, Skills are reusable, modular packages containing custom instructions and context that extend the native capabilities of the Gemini assistant. Think of a skill as a specialized "micro-instruction" or a dedicated tool that you can plug into your chat assistant to make it perform domain-specific tasks instantly—such as scanning legal uploads, rewriting drafts in a corporate brand voice, or formatting structured tickets.

Skills are built using the Open Standard for agentic skills issued by agentskills.io.

Skills vs. No-Code Agents (Agent Workflows)

It is common to confuse Skills with No-Code Agents (built using the Agent Designer). While both customize the assistant’s behavior, they serve entirely different purposes and operate in distinct ways:

Feature/Attribute

Skills

No-Code Agents (Agent Workflows)

Core Concept

Modular, reusable "building blocks" or plugins designed to enhance the primary chat assistant dynamically.

Fully autonomous, end-to-end assistants designed to execute specific, multi-step processes.

Orchestration

Zero-shot routing: Gemini dynamically decides when to call a skill based on its description, or you can invoke it manually.

Operates in a dedicated, isolated agent workspace designed for specific, auditable business workflows.

Scope

Can be called within any conversational chat with the core Gemini assistant. Cannot be called inside custom sub-agents.

Independent entities. They run their own specialized environments and cannot call standard user Skills.

Complexity

Best for single-turn, repetitive tasks (e.g., formatting text, scanning a file, rewriting in brand voice).

Best for complex, multi-stage processes requiring long asynchronous logic.

Examples

Reformatting meeting notes into Track&Release tickets

Transfer meeting transcripts into defined meeting notes and tasks in Track&Release tickets

Reviewing a contract for compliance

Applying brand voice guidelines

Coach / Roast your presentation

A multi-stage research involving multiple human in the loop iterations

Default Google-Managed Skills

Out of the box, Gemini Enterprise includes several pre-built skills developed by Google:

  • Contract Review: Analyzes uploaded legal documents to flag potential liabilities or deviations from standard templates.

  • Customer Briefing: Consolidates customer profiles and recent touchpoints to prepare team members for upcoming client meetings.

  • Project Updates: Summarizes multiple project status reports and key metrics into a clear executive briefing.

2. How to Add Skills & Where to Find Them

To begin managing your skills, log in to the Gemini Enterprise web app and navigate to the Skills tab located in the main sidebar.

Finding Skills

Inside the Browse Skills catalog, you can find and install skills categorized under three sections:

  1. All: A unified repository displaying both pre-configured Google skills and custom skills created by users.

  2. Google: Default, built-in skills managed directly by Google.

  3. Bosch Prompt Gallery: access the Bosch Prompt Gallery from within Gemini Enterprise. Have a look at the announcements overview. (Direct link)

Installing a Browseable Skill

  1. Click Skills in the navigation menu.

  2. Click the Add icon (+) and select Browse skills.

  3. Find the desired skill and click + Install.

Install from Bosch Prompt gallery.

  1. Access the Bosch Prompt Gallery
  2. Select your skill under "My prompts" / "Community prompts" / "Favorite prompts" and click in "copy"
  3. Follow up with the next section "Creating a Custom Skill with Gemini"

Creating a Custom Skill with Gemini

You can build a custom skill natively inside the browser using natural language:

  1. On the Skills page, click the Add icon (+) and select Create skill with Gemini.

  1. Provide a unique Name and a Description.

    • Pro-Tip: The Description is critical. Gemini Enterprise reads this field to determine whether the skill is relevant to a user's prompt. Make sure to include precise "trigger instructions" here.

  2. Write your custom prompt instructions inside the editor using natural language or Markdown formatting.  User should provide detailed instructions on how the skill should work. See the markdowns below to see which sections it should include. 

  3. Click Save/Create. The skill is automatically toggled On by default.

3. How to Import Markdown (.md) Files

If you have downloaded a prompt template (for example, an .md file from the Bosch Prompt Library or a local repository), you can import it directly into Gemini Enterprise.

Step-by-Step Import

  1. Go to the Skills tab, click the Add icon (+), and select Upload Skill (or Import).

  2. Drag and drop or browse for your .md file (or a .zip archive for advanced packages) and click Import.

Packaging Rules

To ensure a successful upload, keep these rules in mind:

  • The Root File: Every upload package must contain a file named skill.md or SKILL.md located at the root directory of your ZIP file or uploaded directly. The platform parses this file to extract the skill's name, description, and operational rules.

  • Advanced ZIP Archiving: For complex execution, you can upload a .zip package. The folder structure should look like this:

    my-custom-skill.zip/
├── skill.md               <-- Main prompt, instructions, and metadata
└── scripts/               <-- Optional folder containing execution scripts
    ├── format_logic.py    <-- Python script
    └── system_check.sh    <-- Bash script

  • Only Python and Bash scripts are supported inside the /scripts directory for running back-end processing logic.

4. How to Prompt with One or Multiple Skills

Once a skill is installed and active (the toggle next to it on the Skills page is On), you can invoke it in your chat sessions in three different ways:

1. Manual Mentions (Shortcuts)

You can directly tell Gemini to run a skill using special characters in the chat box:

  • The Slash (/) Command: Type / in the chat input. A pop-up menu will display all of your active Skills (e.g., /MY AWESOME SKILL).

  • The At (@) Command: Type @ in the chat input. This opens a unified mentions menu containing both your available Skills and Agents.

2. Direct Natural Language Requests

You can simply state your intent in plain language. For example:

"Please use the JIRA Ticket Formatter skill to rewrite my bug description."

3. Automatic Selection (Zero-Shot Routing)

If a skill is toggled on, you do not need to manually call it. When you submit a prompt, Gemini Enterprise automatically evaluates your request against the descriptions of your active skills. If it detects a match, it silently triggers the corresponding skill instructions behind the scenes.

Rules and Key Restraints

  • Skills vs. Agents: You can use multiple skills dynamically in a single conversation, but you cannot invoke both an agent and a skill in the same prompt.

  • No Sub-Agent Calling: Skills cannot be accessed, integrated, or executed from within custom workflows built in the Agent Designer.

5. Writing Your Own Skills: Do's and Don'ts

When designing the core skill.md file, adhere to these prompt engineering best practices:

DO:

  • DO write highly explicit, search-friendly descriptions: Because Gemini Enterprise automatically routes queries based on the description, clearly outline the exact tasks, terms, and keywords that should trigger your skill.

  • DO use structured Markdown layouts: Organize your skill.md with clear headers such as # System Instructions, # Input Variables, # Rules of Engagement, and # Expected Output Format.

  • DO define clear trigger guidelines: Include a specific section in your description stating: "Trigger this skill whenever the user asks to [action]..."

  • DO leverage scripts for processing tasks: If your skill requires complex regex parsing, math computations, or data formatting, bundle a Python script in a ZIP file to handle the heavy lifting.

DON'T:

  • DON'T assume active chat context is used during creation: When using "Create skill with Gemini", the natural language builder cannot pull from your ongoing chat window or read data from active database connectors. Draft your instructions self-contained.

  • DON'T build "all-in-one" monster skills: Keep your skills modular. Instead of a single "Corporate Writing, Legal Review, and Coding Skill", break them down into three separate, modular skills.

  • DON'T expect Model Context Protocol (MCP) support: Skills are not compatible with custom MCP servers integrated within your enterprise dashboard.

6. Practical Examples (4 Use Cases)

Below are five practical examples of how to design and format your skill.md files.


Example 1: Track&Release (JIRA) Bug Ticket Formatter

  • Name: JIRA Ticket Formatter

  • Description: Formats unstructured bug reports into highly structured JIRA tickets. Trigger this skill when the user mentions "make a ticket", "jira bug", or "format issue".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Track&Release Ticket Formatter

## Instructions
Take the raw bug description provided by the user and format it exactly into the following schema:

### Bug Title
[Clear, action-oriented title]

### Steps to Reproduce
1. [Step 1]
2. [Step 2]

### Expected Behavior
[What should have happened]

### Actual Behavior
[What actually happened]

### Environment
- **OS:** Unknown (unless specified)
- **Severity:** [Low / Medium / High / Critical]

Example 2: Technical Documentation Summarizer

  • Name: Technical Summarizer

  • Description: Distills technical specifications and API docs into clear, high-level summaries for product management. Trigger this skill when the user asks to "summarize specs", "explain this API", or "distill technical document".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Technical Summarizer

## Instructions
Review the technical documentation provided and output a 3-part summary:
1. **Executive Summary:** A 2-sentence non-technical overview of what this technology does.
2. **Key Capabilities:** Bulleted list of the top 3-5 developer features.
3. **Integration Requirements:** Quick checklist of prerequisites, dependencies, or authentication requirements.

Example 3: Code Review and Security Analyzer

  • Name: Code Reviewer

  • Description: Audits code blocks for security vulnerabilities, memory leaks, and adherence to standard clean-coding standards. Trigger this skill when the user asks to "review my code", "find bugs in this function", or "check code security".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Code Reviewer Skill

## Instructions
Analyze the user-provided code block. Your response must address:
- **Vulnerabilities:** Flag any unsafe operations (SQL injection, buffer overflow, credentials exposure).
- **Optimization:** Highlight redundant loops, memory leaks, or slow operations.
- **Clean Code:** Suggest stylistic improvements (naming, modularity).

Provide the corrected code block alongside your comments.

Example 4: Meeting Minutes Action-Item Parser

  • Name: Meeting Action-Item Parser

  • Description: Scans raw, transcript-like meeting notes and extracts tasks, assigned owners, and deadlines. Trigger this skill when the user inputs meeting notes or mentions "extract action items" or "who is doing what".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Meeting Action-Item Parser

## Instructions
Examine the meeting transcript. Identify and list all action items using the following format:
- [ ] **Task Description** | **Assignee:** [Name] | **Deadline:** [Date/TBD]

If no assignee or deadline is specified in the text, mark them as "Unassigned" or "TBD" respectively.

7. How to share your skills

When you have tested your skill you can share the skill with:

User circleHow to
individual users
  1. Navigate to skills
  2. Select the skill you want to share
  3. Click on the 3 dots
  4. Click "Share"
  5. Add the individual users in the format userID@bosch.com
  6. Click "done"



bosch wide

Open a ticket in IT-Servicemanagement: 


We need:


Name of the skill:

Purpose:

Co-Owner:


How to open a Ticket for AskBosch powered by Gemini Enterprise

8. Known Limitations

While extremely powerful, Skills in Gemini Enterprise operate with the following constraints:

  • Skills not Available on Agent Designer:  Skills cannot be called or utilized by autonomous workflows built in Agent Designer.

  • UI Transparency Limits: When Gemini automatically triggers a skill behind the scenes, the web interface does not display a badge showing which skills were invoked in generating the final response.

  • Creation Constraints: Skills cannot automatically link to or feed data from connectors (e.g., OneDrive / Sharepoint / eMail).

  • Script Limitations: Only Python and Bash script files are supported in ZIP uploads.

  • Canvas Compatibility: Skills perform best within the side-by-side Canvas interface when they are strictly single-file SKILL.md configurations.

  • No MCP Compatibility: You cannot use custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers within a skill.

  • Basic users not able to create / import skills: You cannot create or important skills in the role of a basic user, this is only possible as advanced user.

9. Troubleshooting

Issue: A skill does not automatically trigger when expected

  • Likely Cause: The description of your skill is too vague, or it lacks key trigger verbs.

  • Solution: Edit the skill on your Skills page. Modify the Description to contain precise keyword instructions (e.g., "Trigger this skill whenever the user says..."). Alternatively, bypass automatic routing by manually calling the skill with / or @.

Issue: Multi-file ZIP scripts do not show up in the web editor

  • Likely Cause: This is a UI limitation. The web editor is only built to display the primary skill.md file.

  • Solution: Your nested scripts (e.g., Python files under /scripts) are still successfully loaded and will execute in the background. If you need to edit code scripts, modify them on your local machine, zip the folder again, and re-import the file.

Issue: Created or shared skills are missing or cannot be invoked

  • Likely Cause: The skills feature or skill sharing has been disabled or suspended by your enterprise administrator, or a shared skill is awaiting admin approval.

  • Solution: Check the status label next to the skill on the Skills page.

    • Private: Visible and usable only by you.

    • Suspended/Disabled: Temporarily deactivated by an administrator. While suspended, you can still edit and test the skill privately, but it cannot be shared or called in public chats.

  • The Root File: Every upload package must contain a file named skill.md or SKILL.md located at the root directory of your ZIP file or uploaded directly. The platform parses this file to extract the skill's name, description, and operational rules.

  • Advanced ZIP Archiving: For complex execution, you can upload a .zip package. The folder structure should look like this:

    my-custom-skill.zip/
├── skill.md               <-- Main prompt, instructions, and metadata
└── scripts/               <-- Optional folder containing execution scripts
    ├── format_logic.py    <-- Python script
    └── system_check.sh    <-- Bash script

  • Only Python and Bash scripts are supported inside the /scripts directory for running back-end processing logic.

4. How to Prompt with One or Multiple Skills

Once a skill is installed and active (the toggle next to it on the Skills page is On), you can invoke it in your chat sessions in three different ways:

1. Manual Mentions (Shortcuts)

You can directly tell Gemini to run a skill using special characters in the chat box:

  • The Slash (/) Command: Type / in the chat input. A pop-up menu will display all of your active Skills (e.g., /MY AWESOME SKILL).

  • The At (@) Command: Type @ in the chat input. This opens a unified mentions menu containing both your available Skills and Agents.

2. Direct Natural Language Requests

You can simply state your intent in plain language. For example:

"Please use the JIRA Ticket Formatter skill to rewrite my bug description."

3. Automatic Selection (Zero-Shot Routing)

If a skill is toggled on, you do not need to manually call it. When you submit a prompt, Gemini Enterprise automatically evaluates your request against the descriptions of your active skills. If it detects a match, it silently triggers the corresponding skill instructions behind the scenes.

Rules and Key Restraints

  • Skills vs. Agents: You can use multiple skills dynamically in a single conversation, but you cannot invoke both an agent and a skill in the same prompt.

  • No Sub-Agent Calling: Skills cannot be accessed, integrated, or executed from within custom workflows built in the Agent Designer.

5. Writing Your Own Skills: Do's and Don'ts

When designing the core skill.md file, adhere to these prompt engineering best practices:

DO:

  • DO write highly explicit, search-friendly descriptions: Because Gemini Enterprise automatically routes queries based on the description, clearly outline the exact tasks, terms, and keywords that should trigger your skill.

  • DO use structured Markdown layouts: Organize your skill.md with clear headers such as # System Instructions, # Input Variables, # Rules of Engagement, and # Expected Output Format.

  • DO define clear trigger guidelines: Include a specific section in your description stating: "Trigger this skill whenever the user asks to [action]..."

  • DO leverage scripts for processing tasks: If your skill requires complex regex parsing, math computations, or data formatting, bundle a Python script in a ZIP file to handle the heavy lifting.

DON'T:

  • DON'T assume active chat context is used during creation: When using "Create skill with Gemini", the natural language builder cannot pull from your ongoing chat window or read data from active database connectors. Draft your instructions self-contained.

  • DON'T build "all-in-one" monster skills: Keep your skills modular. Instead of a single "Corporate Writing, Legal Review, and Coding Skill", break them down into three separate, modular skills.

  • DON'T expect Model Context Protocol (MCP) support: Skills are not compatible with custom MCP servers integrated within your enterprise dashboard.

6. Practical Examples (4 Use Cases)

Below are five practical examples of how to design and format your skill.md files.


Example 1: Track&Release (JIRA) Bug Ticket Formatter

  • Name: JIRA Ticket Formatter

  • Description: Formats unstructured bug reports into highly structured JIRA tickets. Trigger this skill when the user mentions "make a ticket", "jira bug", or "format issue".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Track&Release Ticket Formatter

## Instructions
Take the raw bug description provided by the user and format it exactly into the following schema:

### Bug Title
[Clear, action-oriented title]

### Steps to Reproduce
1. [Step 1]
2. [Step 2]

### Expected Behavior
[What should have happened]

### Actual Behavior
[What actually happened]

### Environment
- **OS:** Unknown (unless specified)
- **Severity:** [Low / Medium / High / Critical]

Example 2: Technical Documentation Summarizer

  • Name: Technical Summarizer

  • Description: Distills technical specifications and API docs into clear, high-level summaries for product management. Trigger this skill when the user asks to "summarize specs", "explain this API", or "distill technical document".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Technical Summarizer

## Instructions
Review the technical documentation provided and output a 3-part summary:
1. **Executive Summary:** A 2-sentence non-technical overview of what this technology does.
2. **Key Capabilities:** Bulleted list of the top 3-5 developer features.
3. **Integration Requirements:** Quick checklist of prerequisites, dependencies, or authentication requirements.

Example 3: Code Review and Security Analyzer

  • Name: Code Reviewer

  • Description: Audits code blocks for security vulnerabilities, memory leaks, and adherence to standard clean-coding standards. Trigger this skill when the user asks to "review my code", "find bugs in this function", or "check code security".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Code Reviewer Skill

## Instructions
Analyze the user-provided code block. Your response must address:
- **Vulnerabilities:** Flag any unsafe operations (SQL injection, buffer overflow, credentials exposure).
- **Optimization:** Highlight redundant loops, memory leaks, or slow operations.
- **Clean Code:** Suggest stylistic improvements (naming, modularity).

Provide the corrected code block alongside your comments.

Example 4: Meeting Minutes Action-Item Parser

  • Name: Meeting Action-Item Parser

  • Description: Scans raw, transcript-like meeting notes and extracts tasks, assigned owners, and deadlines. Trigger this skill when the user inputs meeting notes or mentions "extract action items" or "who is doing what".

  • File Template (skill.md):

    # Meeting Action-Item Parser

## Instructions
Examine the meeting transcript. Identify and list all action items using the following format:
- [ ] **Task Description** | **Assignee:** [Name] | **Deadline:** [Date/TBD]

If no assignee or deadline is specified in the text, mark them as "Unassigned" or "TBD" respectively.

8. Known Limitations

While extremely powerful, Skills in Gemini Enterprise operate with the following constraints:

  • Skills not Available on Agent Designer:  Skills cannot be called or utilized by autonomous workflows built in Agent Designer.

  • UI Transparency Limits: When Gemini automatically triggers a skill behind the scenes, the web interface does not display a badge showing which skills were invoked in generating the final response.

  • Creation Constraints: Skills cannot automatically link to or feed data from connectors (e.g., OneDrive / Sharepoint / eMail).

  • Script Limitations: Only Python and Bash script files are supported in ZIP uploads.

  • Canvas Compatibility: Skills perform best within the side-by-side Canvas interface when they are strictly single-file SKILL.md configurations.

  • No MCP Compatibility: You cannot use custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers within a skill.

  • Basic users not able to create / import skills: You cannot create or important skills in the role of a basic user, this is only possible as advanced user.

9. Troubleshooting

Issue: A skill does not automatically trigger when expected

  • Likely Cause: The description of your skill is too vague, or it lacks key trigger verbs.

  • Solution: Edit the skill on your Skills page. Modify the Description to contain precise keyword instructions (e.g., "Trigger this skill whenever the user says..."). Alternatively, bypass automatic routing by manually calling the skill with / or @.

Issue: Multi-file ZIP scripts do not show up in the web editor

  • Likely Cause: This is a UI limitation. The web editor is only built to display the primary skill.md file.

  • Solution: Your nested scripts (e.g., Python files under /scripts) are still successfully loaded and will execute in the background. If you need to edit code scripts, modify them on your local machine, zip the folder again, and re-import the file.

Issue: Created or shared skills are missing or cannot be invoked

  • Likely Cause: The skills feature or skill sharing has been disabled or suspended by your enterprise administrator, or a shared skill is awaiting admin approval.

  • Solution: Check the status label next to the skill on the Skills page.

    • Private: Visible and usable only by you.

    • Suspended/Disabled: Temporarily deactivated by an administrator. While suspended, you can still edit and test the skill privately, but it cannot be shared or called in public chats.

Understanding Dependency Resolution

At its core, dependency resolution is the process of identifying and installing all the packages that your project needs to run. When you install a Python package, that package might in turn depend on other packages, which themselves have their own dependencies. This creates a "dependency tree". A dependency manager's job is to navigate this tree and install versions of each package that are compatible with all the others.

The Standard Tool: pip

The most common tool for managing Python packages is pip, which is included with modern Python installations. When you run pip install, it reads the dependencies of the requested package and attempts to install them.

How pip Resolves Dependencies

pip's dependency resolver is capable of "backtracking." This means that if it installs a version of a package that conflicts with another package's requirements, it will go back and try a different version until it finds a compatible set. This process can sometimes look like pip is downloading multiple versions of the same package, which is normal behavior.

While pip is the standard, it has some limitations. For instance, it doesn't have a built-in mechanism to distinguish between the packages you explicitly requested and their transitive dependencies, which can sometimes lead to a cluttered environment. This has led to the development of more advanced tools.


Modern Dependency Management Tools

To address the limitations of pip and provide a more robust workflow, several modern tools have emerged. These tools typically offer more features, such as project management, virtual environment handling, and deterministic dependency locking.

Here's a look at some of the most popular ones:

Poetry: The All-in-One Solution

Poetry is a very popular tool that handles dependency management, packaging, and virtual environments. It uses two key files:

  • pyproject.toml: This file is used to declare your project's metadata and dependencies. You can specify version constraints for your dependencies in this file

  • poetry.lock: This file locks your dependencies to specific versions. When you run poetry install, it uses the exact versions from this file, ensuring that your environment is reproducible across different machines. You should commit this file to your version control.


With Poetry, you can manage your dependencies with commands like poetry add <package> and poetry remove <package>. It also provides dependency groups to separate development dependencies from your main project dependencies.

uv: The Fast Newcomer

uv is a newer, extremely fast package manager written in Rust. It's designed to be a drop-in replacement for pip and pip-tools, and it's often 10-100x faster. uv can also manage virtual environments, making it an all-in-one tool for many Python workflows. It is rapidly gaining popularity and is a great choice for new projects.

Other Notable Tools

  • PDM (Python Development Master): Similar to Poetry, PDM focuses on following Python's packaging standards (PEPs) as closely as possible.

  • Hatch: This tool is particularly strong for package development and offers flexible environment management.

  • Rye: Rye aims to be an all-encompassing Python project management tool, handling everything from Python installation to publishing packages.


Comparison of Popular Tools

Dependency ResolutionYesYes (with locking)Yes (with locking)
Virtual Environment ManagementNo (requires venv)YesYes
Project ManagementNoYesYes
Lock FileNo (requires pip-tools)poetry.lockuv.lock
SpeedStandardGood

Extremely Fast


Recommendations

  • For beginners and simple projects: Using pip with venv and a requirements.txt file is a great way to start.

  • For most new projects: uv is an excellent choice due to its speed and all-in-one nature. 

  • For established, complex projects: Poetry is a mature and robust option with a large community and extensive documentation.


The venv module in Python is a crucial tool for creating and managing isolated Python environments. It's built into Python 3.3 and later, meaning you don't need to install anything extra to use it.

What is a Virtual Environment?

Imagine you're working on multiple Python projects on the same machine.

  • Project A needs Django==3.2 and requests==2.20.

  • Project B needs Django==4.1 (because it uses a newer feature) and requests==2.28.

If you were to install these packages globally, you'd run into conflicts. Installing Django==3.2 then Django==4.1 would overwrite the previous version, breaking Project A.

A virtual environment solves this by creating a self-contained directory that has its own Python interpreter and its own set of installed packages. This means:

  • Isolation: Each project can have its own dependencies installed without interfering with other projects or the system-wide Python installation.

  • Reproducibility: You can define the exact dependencies for a project in a requirements.txt file (or similar), and anyone else working on the project can create an identical environment.

  • Cleanliness: It keeps your global Python installation clean and free from project-specific packages.


How to Use venv

Here's a typical workflow for using venv:

1. Create a Virtual Environment

Navigate to your project directory in your terminal and run:

python -m venv my_project_env

  • python -m venv: This tells Python to run the venv module.

  • my_project_env: This is the name of the directory where your virtual environment will be created. You can choose any name, but common practices include venv, .venv, or env.

This command creates a directory (e.g., my_project_env/) that contains:

  • A copy of the Python interpreter.

  • The pip installer.

  • Directories for installing packages.


2. Activate the Virtual Environment

Before you can use the isolated environment, you need to "activate" it. The activation process adjusts your shell's PATH variable so that when you run python or pip, it points to the versions within your virtual environment, not the global ones.

On Windows (Command Prompt):
my_project_env\Scripts\activate.bat

On Windows (PowerShell):
my_project_env\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Once activated, your terminal prompt will usually change to indicate that you are inside the virtual environment (e.g., (my_project_env) yourusername@yourmachine:~/my_project$).


3. Install Packages


With the virtual environment activated, you can now install project-specific packages using pip:

 
pip install Django requests

These packages will be installed only within my_project_env and will not affect your global Python installation.

4. Deactivate the Virtual Environment

When you're done working on your project, you can deactivate the virtual environment:

deactivate

Your terminal prompt will return to its normal state, and your python and pip commands will once again refer to the global Python installation (or another activated virtual environment if you have nested them, though that's less common).


Why is venv Important?

  • Dependency Management: Prevents conflicts between different projects needing different versions of the same library.

  • Project Portability: Makes it easy to share your project. You can generate a requirements.txt file (using pip freeze > requirements.txt) that lists all installed packages and their versions. Others can then create an identical environment by running pip install -r requirements.txt within their own virtual environment.

  • Development Best Practice: It's considered a fundamental best practice in Python development to use virtual environments for every project.

  • Testing: Ensures that your code runs only with the intended dependencies, preventing subtle bugs caused by accidentally using globally installed libraries.

In essence, venv empowers you to create a controlled and consistent development environment for each of your Python projects, leading to fewer headaches and more reliable code.

Table of Contents

  1. Introduction
  2. Install NI driver
  3. Set device name
  4. Install required python packages

  5. Two different ways to drive currents of more than 1mA with NI6501

  6. Start up configuration
  7. Python script

Introduction

The NI USB-6501 is an expensive (~115€) USB connected module providing GPIO capability
to Windows PCs.

Install NI driver

Download the driver from:
http://www.ni.com/de-de/support/model.usb-6501.html
Install it.

Set device name

Open the NI Measurement & Automation Explorer and set the device name to "TestDevice".
If you use another name you need to modify the python script accessing the device accordingly.


Install required python packages

Use python package manager pip to install numpy and pydaqmx python packages:

py -3 -m pip install numpy pydaqmx

(you need to execute this command in an admin console and be connected to a non-bsh network)

Two different ways to drive currents of more than 1mA with NI6501

One way is to set the GPIOs to active drive mode the other is to use an external pull-up resistor of <2.2 kOhms
between VCC and the GPIO. The python example below uses the active drive mod eto drive the relais.


Start up configuration

At start-up the GPIOs are set to High with a 4,7 kOhms Pull-up Resistor, which is not enough to drive a relais.
The solution to put the relais in default on mode is to either actively set the state to on in active drive by software or
to use an external pull-up resistor. The power up state of the NI6501 is not internally programmable!

Python output demo script

The script below will set "Port1 pin7" / GPIO3 periodically to High and Low,
each phase lasting for one second.

CreateDOChan(...)

In order to use another name than "TestDevice", the first argument in CreateDOChan function needs to be modified accordingly.
The device has 3 groups of GPIOs named port 0, port 1 and port 2. To specify the port group to use, modify the first argument
accordingly. If the line part in the first argument is omitted, all lines of the given port will be available for writing.

task.SetDOOutputDriveType("line7", PyDAQmx.DAQmx_Val_ActiveDrive)

The GPIOs can be setup in two different ways, push-pull and open-collector. In the standard open-collector mode
a pull-up resistor of 4,7 kOhms is used which limits the current to below 0,4 mA.
To drive a relais a current of around 1mA is needed, which is too much for the standard open-collector mode.
More current is available is in push-pull (activedrive) mode, which can provide up to 8,5 mA.
To set the GPIO in ActiveDrive mode use the function call above.

WriteDigitalLines(...)

The arguments of this function are: 

  • numSampsPerChan  int32: The number of samples, per channel, to write. You must pass in a value of 0 or more in order for the sample to write. If you pass a negative number, this function returns an error.
  • autoStart  bool32: Specifies whether or not this function automatically starts the task if you do not start it.
  • timeout  float64: The amount of time, in seconds, to wait for this function to write all the samples. To specify an infinite wait, pass -1 (DAQmx_Val_WaitInfinitely). This function returns an error if the timeout elapses.
    A value of 0 indicates to try once to write the submitted samples. If this function successfully writes all submitted samples, it does not return an error. Otherwise, the function returns a timeout error and returns the number of samples actually written.
  • dataLayout  bool32: Specifies how the samples are arranged, either interleaved or noninterleaved. Value  Description
    DAQmx_Val_GroupByChannel   Group by channel (noninterleaved)
    DAQmx_Val_GroupByScanNumber   Group by sample (interleaved)
  • writeArray  uInt8 [] : The samples to write to the task.
  • sampsPerChanWritten int32 *
  • reserved bool32 *


Python output demo
import numpy as np
import PyDAQmx
import time

data0 = np.array([0], dtype=np.uint8)
data1 = np.array([1], dtype=np.uint8)

task = PyDAQmx.Task()
task.CreateDOChan("/TestDevice/port1/line7", "line7", PyDAQmx.DAQmx_Val_ChanForAllLines)

# Set channel to open-drain = push-pull / active drive, -> larger max GPIO current
task.SetDOOutputDriveType("line7", PyDAQmx.DAQmx_Val_ActiveDrive)

task.StartTask()

# Cycle 10 times
for i in range(10):
    # Write Low data0
    task.WriteDigitalLines(1,0,-1,PyDAQmx.DAQmx_Val_GroupByChannel,data0,None,None)
    print("Output Low")
    time.sleep(1)

    # Write High data1
    task.WriteDigitalLines(1,0,-1,PyDAQmx.DAQmx_Val_GroupByChannel,data1,None,None)
    print("Output High")
    time.sleep(1)

task.StopTask()

This guide explains how to flash the ECU (B-sample) using winIDEA. To start flashing the sample image, the elf and hex files must be prepared. These files can be generated from ifx_tc4_bswkit.

The software files can be cloned from the following repository: ifx_tc4_bswkit

git clone https://github.boschdevcloud.com/XC-CE/ifx_tc4_bswkit.git

1. How to Install ToolBase SW

To launch ToolBase SW, you need to request access on the following platforms:

  1. IT Service Portal:
    ToolBase Access Request
    Request: Toolbase
  2. Service Registration:
    ToolBase Client User Registration
    Request: Toolbase Client User

After getting approval, open the hidden icons from the bottom right taskbar and launch tb (toolbase client).

Using ToolBase Environment Explorer, the Green Hills Compiler for IFX (for Infineon Automotive Microcontrollers) can be updated or installed by following the steps below:

2. How to Build toyota_cgw

2.1. Check Python Version

After successfully installing ToolBase SW, please check your Python version.

Attention: If your Python version is 3.9 or higher, please ignore this section and proceed directly to 2.2. Install all the required SW.

python --version

If the output only shows Python without a version number, it probably means the Python App Execution Alias (Microsoft Store stub) is responding. Run the following command to check:

where python

If the output is:

C:\\Users\\MTA7YH\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\WindowsApps\\python.exe

This indicates that the actual Python is not installed, and only the Store stub is present. You must install the official Python release (recommended version: Python 3.9 or higher):

Python 3.14 Official Download

Note: During installation, ensure that the checkbox "Add python.exe to PATH" is checked so that python.exe can be referenced from any directory on your local PC.

If the command python --version is still not executable in VS Code even after passing the path, try running the following command to set the path environment variable temporarily:

$env:PATH = "C:\Users\MTA7YH\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python314;C:\Users\MTA7YH\AppData\Local\Programs\Python\Python314\Scripts;" + $env:PATH

2.2. Install Required Software

Install all required software necessary to compile the TCGW project by executing .\start_tbu.bat.

cd tools\tbu\
.\start_tbu.bat

start_tbu.bat executes the following two phases:

Phase 1: Initialization of ToolBase environment

  1. Environment Configuration: Configure ps.ec.cloud.build.tools to the current environment.
  2. Perl Activation: perl/5.14.4.1_3a_ecl is activated.
  3. Update Local Metadata: Confirm 18 environments (such as ae.be, cc, misc, ps.ec.cloud.build.tools).

Phase 2: Confirm the project-specific tools

RECENT CHANGES TO WINDOWS MIGHT BREAK SERVICE IN SOME MACHINES. AS THE SERVICE CAN'T AUTOSTART PROPERLY.

PLEASE USE RB LOCAL PROXY MANAGER INSTEAD

Background

Every request going to the internet from within Bosch will be blocked unless we have some account attached to the request. To attach our account into each request, the standard way is to use proxy.

Each region in Bosch have one primary proxy and usually already configured if using software installed by CI (chrome, firefox, anaconda, ....). If we use our own software downloaded from the internet (nodejs-npm, python-pip, gradle, maven,...) we will have to configure the proxy our self.

Inner working

Most of the time we only using two proxy endpoints:

  • For APAC region (Singapore, Vietnam, India, ...) rb-proxy-apac.bosch.com:8080
  • For DE region (Germany, ...)  rb-proxy-de.bosch.com:8080

Using the above proxy end points we can authenticate our request using the following URL http://<username>:<password>@rb-proxy-apac.bosch.com:8080

<username> and <password> will be the same one you used to login into windows. The final URL will look something like this http://rph2hc:mywindowpasswd123@rb-proxy-apac.bosch.com:8080

The above approach have several issues:

  1. The approach is not encouraged as it expose username and password.
  2. When password changed, we need to go through each configured application to change the password.

Solution

To combat those issues we will install proxy software such as PX to automate the proxy endpoint fetching and proxy authentication.

If you are from Vietnam then every thing is configured. If you are not from Vietnam you will want to correct pac field in px.ini for optimal performance.


3. Install

PythonVirtualenvOperator

pythonvirtualenvoperator

    requirements=['plotly>=4.7.0'],
    system_site_packages=False,

This guide explains how Conan can be installed as a Python package via the Pip package manager.

Prerequisites

  • Python (version >= 3.6)
  • Valid API key for the on-premise JFrog Artifactory (Edit Profile > API Key)

Pip Authentication

Depending on which OS you use, you may use different ways for authentication:

  • Basic HTTP authentication
  • .netrc file
  • Keyring provider

To see the detailed guide for each option, please refer to the official Pip documentation.

If you are using a Linux/UNIX OS, the .netrc file is the preferred way.

However, the easiest way is to use Basic HTTP authentication. An example will be provided below.

Installing Conan from the Bosch-internal Pip Mirror

Instead of installing Conan from an repository outside of Bosch (e.g., pypi.org), the official way is to use the on-prem JFrog Artifactory mirror to install Python packages.

The JFrog Artifactory URL to resolve and download Python packages within Bosch is: https://rb-artifactory.bosch.com/artifactory/api/pypi/python-remote/simple (clicking the link will result in a 404 error; be assured that it is valid though).

In order to install a Python package from a specific repository you need to pass the --index-url option. To install Conan, use the command below:

Via .netrc File

If you have a .netrc configuration file the authentication is already set up.

pip install --index-url="https://rb-artifactory.bosch.com/artifactory/api/pypi/python-remote/simple" conan

Via Basic HTTP Authentication

If you do not have a .netrc configuration file you can provide the username and password to the --index-url option as shown below:

https://username:password@pypi.company.com/simple

In this case this would result in the following command to download Conan:

pip install --index-url="https://<nt-user>:<api-key>@rb-artifactory.bosch.com/artifactory/api/pypi/python-remote/simple" conan

Installing Specific Conan Versions

The above commands will always install the latest Conan version available. See the examples below if you wish to install another, specific version.

pip install --index-url="..." conan==2.3.0 # Specific Conan 2 version
pip install --index-url="..." conan<2 # Latest Conan 1 version

Description

This page describes how in general additional Python modules (aka libs) can be installed on a developers or server machine.  In the child page all the concrete additional modules are listed that are required to be installed on every machine where the VRTE software build is running.

No details please just tell me what to do!

If you just want to know which/how to install the Python modules go to: Required Python modules for local script/tool execution.

Why additional Python modules?

In order to not run reimplement functionality that is available for free via specific (OSS or free) Python modules they have to be installed on every machine that will be running these tools. VRTE System team has developed new tools or has enhanced tools that make use of these Python modules.

Why not install them automatically?

Python modules could also be installed automatically by the tool that needs them but due to following reasons this is not done:

  • A developer should be able to decide on his/her own whether he/she needs/wants some additional Python module or not. VRTE System team does not want to overwrite any potentially existing configuration of your installed Python distribution.
  • The effort for installing the modules is so simple and needs to be done only once (per used Python distribution)

Steps for Windows Users

  1. Ensure you have toolbase installed via SCCM. If not request for it in the IT-Service Portal.
    Hint:     Annaconda Python via SCCM is broken regarding the Azure modules. Use toolbase.
  2. Installl in the environment cdg.de python 3.8.1.0.0 either in the Toolbase Explorer GUI or via command line:

  3. Execute following

    Windows Shell commands
    rem Activate the next two lines (by removing 'rem') in case the below pip install command aborts with a proxy error
rem set "HTTP_PROXY="
rem set "HTTPS_PROXY="
tbexcmd -useEnv:cdg.de -command EnableTool python/3.8.1.0.0
tbupdate -exec -showprogress
tini -useEnv:cdg.de python=3.8.1.0.0
pip install module1 module2 module3

Internet Connection Not Required

No dedicated internet proxy configuration is necessary. But if you have configured/setup a proxy wrongly (e.g. without proper exception for bosch.com) the pip command may fail. In this case stop any local proxy (like Px, Cntlm), unset any http(s)_proxy environment variables and try again.

Steps for Linux Users

  1. Install a Python 3.X > 3.6 distribution on your Linux machine if it is not there.
    Hint: In Linux Python 3.x is usually installed in parallel to Python 2.x, therefore the commands have a "3" at the end. Please ensure you have at least Python 3.6 or newer installed.
    Hint: Lower 3.x versions might work as well but has not been tested.

  2. Execute the following command in the shell

    Linux shell commands
    pip3 install module1 module2 module3

Internet Connection Required

When you have OSD (>=4) installed there should be no problem with proxy settings. Otherwise contact the OSD support. If you have installed another Python distribution ensure your proxy setup is correct to provide internet access if required.

How to verify installation was successfull

After installation test whether the new modules can be used. In the below example the additional modules that were installed are azure-cli and azure-devops, e.g. for Windows users (after tini):

python

Python 3.8.1 (tags/v3.8.1:1b293b6, Dec 18 2019, 23:11:46) [MSC v.1916 64 bit (AMD64)] on win32
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> import azure
>>>

Hint: Under Linux likely call is "python3".

What's Miniforge?

Miniforge is a minimal, open-source installer for Conda, an open-source tool used to manage isolated Python environments and binary software packages.

Learn more: GitHub - conda-forge/miniforge

How to start working with Miniforge with the use of Visual Studio Code?


StepWhat to doScreenshot/Link

1

Install Miniforge from IT Service Portal.

Link to the portal: Add/Remove Software - Enterprise IT Hub

2

Check if Miniforge is installed (usually installation is done in couple of hours and might need a PC restart).

  1. Open CMD - use Windows + R and run 'cmd'.
  2. Type:
    conda info
  3. You should see Miniforge environment and config files available.

3

Open VS Code.


4

Install 'Python' extension for VS Code.

  1. Go to 'Extensions' tab (icon in the left sidebar).
  2. Search for 'Python'.
  3. Install ' Python' extension.

5

Open Terminal in VS Code with Ctrl + ` or with toolbar.

6

Initialize conda for shell interaction by running command in the Terminal:

conda init powershell


VS Code might need to be restarted after the initialization.

7

Download environment config file and create new virtual environment by running command in the Terminal:

conda create --file <Drive>:\path\to\ibm-pa_environment.yml

When conda asks you to proceed, type y:

proceed ([y]/n)?

New environment will be named ibm-pa.


NOTE: If environment called 'ibm-pa' already exists in conda environments directory, it will be removed and created from scratch.


Learn more about virtual environments:  Managing environments — conda

Environment config file:

ibm-pa_environment.yml


Creation start:


End of the creation process:

8

Set VS Code Python interpreter:

  1. Use combo Ctrl + Shift + P.
  2. Search and select 'Python: Select Interpreter'.
  3. Click 'Enter interpreter path...'.
  4. Provide path to interpreter from newly created env and hit enter:
    C:\Users\<your_user>\.conda\envs\ibm-pa\python.exe


This setup enables running .py scripts with VS Code inbuilt run button .

9

Test Python configuration by generating the Model Map

  1. Download script file extract_tm1_structure_MapOnly.py
  2. Copy the script file to PA-Code folder
  3. Select the script in VSCode left pane
  4. Press 'Run Python File' button
  5. When the script starts correctly, you will be prompted to provide in the VSCode Terminal window:
    1. Username (including domain: <Domain>\<Username>)
    2. Password
    3. Environment
    4. HTTP Port (you can check your TM1 instance HTTP Port here: Instance Overview)
    5. Target folder within the PA-Code folder where your instance is stored (by default: <Admin Host>/<TM1 Instance Name>)
  6. When script finishes, you should see 'Model_Map.md' file in the target folder

10 (optional - hints)

if you want to use 'ibm-pa' environment in PS Terminal, you need to activate it by:

conda activate ibm-pa


Environment can be deactivated by:

conda deactivate

11 (optional - hints)

Terminal default activated environment setup.

It is possible to define default activated Python environment for PS Terminals in two ways:

  1. Inbuilt VS Code function (overrides second option).
    1. By default environment related to the selected interpreter is being activated.
    2. You can set this option:
      1. Use Ctrl + , combo.
      2. Search for 'python activate environmrnt'
      3. Check option 'Activate Python Environment in all Terminals created.'.
  2. Setting conda config (make sure option 1 is disabled).
    1. Use command:
      conda config --set auto_activate true
conda config --set default_activation_env ibm-pa

Conda config is set to activate base env by default. It is cleaner to deactivate this automatic activation with:

conda config --set auto_activate false

If you want to switch default env in conda config from ibm-pa back to base, run:

conda config --set default_activation_env base

1. Introducción.

Encontraras los pasos para instalar Python, también los primeros pasos con Python y Visual Studio Code.


2. Instalación.

  1. Para instalar python, se puede hacer por medio de la plataforma de BD "IT Service portal" con el ticket Add/Remove Software, busca el software Anaconda Python,y selecciona para instalar. Para terminar de generar el ticket da click en los siguientes botones "Calculate Price" (no tiene costo) y "Request".
  2. Instala Microsoft Visual Studio Code (selecciona la opción con proxy), también se encuentra en la lista de software

Anaconda es una distribución de software libre y de código abierto para los lenguajes Python y R, son ayudara a gestionar los entornos de Python.

Microsoft Visual Studio Code, es un editor de código para diferentes tipos de lenguajes de programación, con el podremos hacer y ejecutar los scripts de python.


Ambos programas están en la lista de Software distribuidos por BD, los puedes instalar desde Add/Remove Software, no se requieren derechos de administrador.



3. Instala la extencion de Python en Visual Studio Code,

  • En "Extensions" busca python.
  • Selecciona la opción Python, como lo muestra en la imagen de referencia.
  • da click en el boton "Install".

3. Como crear un entorno de Python.

1. Abre el "Anaconda Prompt"

 

2. Crea un nuevo entorno de python, usa el siguiente comando:

conda create --prefix [path] python=[version] -y

  • [path]: es la ruta en donde se almacenara el entorno, la direccion incluye el nombre del entorno.
  • [version]: es el numero de la distribución de python.
  • [-y]: utilizarla es opcional, sirve para validar una pregunta, en este caso continua con la descarga e instalación del entorno.

ejemplo:

conda create --prefix C:\Users\CED2SLP\.conda\envs\pipelines python=3.11 -y


Como estándar en TEF4, los entornos los guardamos en la siguiente ruta: C:\Users\[user]\.conda\envs\

 

3. Activa el entorno, una ves que termina de crear el entorno te muestra los paquetes que descargo por default y el comando para activar el entorno, puedes copiar y pegar el comando en el prompt.



Comandos para Anaconda y Python: CONDA CHEAT SHEET


Ejemplo de algunos comandos básicos.

. Comando
Activar entorno de Python (usando Anaconda) conda activate nombre_del_entorno
Instalas librerías pip install nombre_de_la_libreria
Consultar librerías instaladas pip list
Consultar la versión de Python python --version
 

4. Como trabajar Python en Visual Studio Code.

1. Abre Visual Studio Code.

2. Agrega una carpeta.


 

3. Crea un nuevo archivo con la extencion .py


 

4. Escribe el script.

 

5. Selecciona el entorno de Python.

  • En la parte inferior derecha se encuentra la opción para seleccionar el entorno.
  • da click sobre la opción Interprete.
 
  • selecciona "Enter interprete path..."
  • despues selecciona "Find..."

  • Busca el interprete y seleccionalo.
 
  • En la parte inferior derecha se encuentra el interprete seleccionado.
 

6. Ejecuta el Script de Python.

  • En la parte superior derecha se encuentra la opción para ejecutar el Script.
