Reproducible FlexDevice Builds on Windows, Linux & GitHub Actions

In vehicle integration, we use FlexDevice (a.ka. FL3XDevice) gateways to map signals between vehicle buses (CAN, Automotive Ethernet, FlexRay). This allows us to run identical Bosch ECU software (like the platform MPC4) on different vehicles. However, our development workflow faced three pain points which my team, GitHub copilot, and I successfully addressed (in PR18 and PR21):
✅ Linux developers can now build FlexDevice firmware without requiring a Windows machine.
✅ Firmware builds are now reproducible. Identical inputs generate identical outputs, making validation, traceability and release management significantly easier.
✅ GitHub Actions can automatically build and publish firmware artifacts, eliminating the need to store generated binaries in Git repositories. Everyone can now access updates to mapping without needing to install FL3XConfig and compiling themselves.

I wanted to share this here for everyone in vehicle integration and would also like to have a discussion about further use-cases. The solution for reproducible builds can also be used for other engineering tools. If you are interested in how Copilot assist in this endeavor (1.5 working days total dev. time), reach out.

⏱️ Quick Guide to Reproducible Builds
For reproducible builds on Windows, download the "windows-clock.zip", unpack it anywhere, and run the following. It will generate the .s19 and .fpga files in the project directory.
windows-clock.exe "C:\Program Files\StarCooperation\FL3X Config 1.5.4.0\FL3XConfigConsole.exe" path\to\project.fcr -build
Solution 1: Linux Support

Together with GitHub copilot, I was able to run the application via the wine compatibility layer and created a multi-stage Dockerfile. Conceptually, this Dockerfile does the following:
Install required tools such as the wine compatibility layer and dotnet runtimes
Install FlexConfig from the official installer. This required some hacks such as manually extracting an MSI from the EXE installer and running one particular installer within a virtual display (Xvfb) as it required a GUI.
Patch a JSON configuration file provided by FL3XConfig because paths prefixed with .\ did not work on wine
Using a launcher script, convert all relative Linux path to absolute Windows paths before running FL3XConfigConsole.exe under Wine.
Doing all of the above in Docker is nice because I do not need to redistribute any software myself and the entire process is automated and transparent. Documentation is also not required. It should be simple to migrate to an updated FL3XConfig version.


Solution 2: Reproducible Builds

Reproducible firmware builds have a huge number of advantages that will only grow as we make more of our test vehicles software defined (see this site for details). For example, if the firmware is binary-identical, there is no need to reflash a device in the test vehicle. It is also trivial to find out which commit-ID was used to generate a specific firmware if one maintains a table of git commits and software versions. There are three sources of non-determinism in FL3XConfig builds:
The computer name (hostname) is included in the build file
Autogenerated header files contain defines (e.g., TIMESTAMP_LOW) with the current system time
The firmware packaging step uses the modification time of autogenerated source files and writes this timestamp information into the firmware image.
I chose to hold the environment constant for the final version, but also had a Python script that used objcopy to null all timestamps in the firmware. Directly patching the binary firmware seemed like a horrible way to get impossible-to-debug segfaults or even brick our FlexDevices. Our solution is simple to explain, but not to implement: (1.) make hostname constant, (2.) fix the system time to an arbitrary value for FL3XConfigConsole.exe and all subprocesses, and (3.) set constant file modification times.

Solution 2 on Linux

I had to make wine run with faked system times, which wine really did not like. Thus, I had to add a warmup step wherein I started wine server with the real system time, but then called it again with faked time.

I mostly used libfaketime, but this did not cover some of the 32-bit system calls used by the mixed 32- and 64-bit exe, resulting in non-constant mtimes. So Copilot and I wrote libconstanttime. Basically, libfaketime and libconstanttime are loaded before all other dymanic libraries (via LD_PRELOAD) and replace time functions with a version that gets the constant from the SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH environment variable. All of this LD_PRELOAD setting is handled in the FL3XConfigClock.sh launcher script.

Solution 2 on Windows

Most FL3XConfig users are still on Windows and I wanted them to also build firmware determinstically. Furthermore, this determinstic build allows me to verify that the firmware built by my Frankenstein linux solution is bit-identical to the windows build. I created a flexconfig-clock.exe file, which can be prefixed to FL3XConfigConsole.exe. In absence of LD_PRELOAD, I used Microsoft Detours to redirect Windows API calls. It was somewhat complex for Copilot and myself as we had to redirect 32-bit and 64-bit calls.

For good measure, I cross-compile flexconfig-console on a GitHub actions Linux runner so that users can simply download the exe file. Interestingly, this windows launcher slows builds from 2-3 minutes to over 8 minutes.

Solution 3: Building with GitHub actions
As I had a Linux docker container, it was rather simple to define this GitHub actions workflow. It downloads the FL3XConfig installer, builds the Dockerfile, runs the Dockerfile, and uploads the artifacts (.s19, .bin, .fpga) and build logs. It runs in parallel for every .fcr file found.
